Testimony of Rep. Adam Lee presenting
LD 45, An Act Allowing the Department of Corrections to Offset Some of the
Costs of Technology Provided to Residents of Correctional Facilities
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice & Public Safety

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety, I am Adam Lee, and I represent House District 89 which is Downtown Auburn and New Auburn. I'm here to introduce LD 45, An Act
Allowing the Department of Corrections to offset some of the Costs of Technology Provided to
Residents of Correctional Facilities.

This is a Department of Corrections bill, and the Department is here with substantially more information and detail than I have, and so I'll ask that you defer your questions for them. I will,
however, briefly explain to you why I agreed to sponsor this bill.

Upon hearing its name and a request that I sponsor it, I was skeptical. As many of you know, for
the past 3 years I have helped to coach the Maine State Prison's Debate team. I coach that team in conjunction with the National Prison Debate League. It's through conversations with the folks
from the NPDL that I've learned just how exemplary Maine is in comparison to other states in providing technological and educational opportunities for residents. We truly are ahead of the curve. My chief concern in seeing the title of the bill is that the Department intended to take
something that it is excellent and is presently being provided to residents for free and charge
them for it. My sponsorship is based on a few understandings, each of which I'd invite you to
challenge the Department on.
First, my understanding is that this bill is not intended to supplant DOC attempts to fund these
programs through available grants or other resources, it's to supplement that funding. Second,
my sponsorship is based on the guarantee that residents will not be charged for their use of
technology in conjunction with their own criminal defense or involvement in civil law suits.
Third, my sponsorship is based on the assurance that the inability to pay for the service will not
preclude someone from using it and will not preclude them from being selected to participate in programs like debate, which require use of the technology. Fourth, I spoke to the department and genuinely believe that there will be some element of empowerment for residents if the service is, in part, funded by the residents. It will be a heck of a lot more difficult to ignore residents'
concerns about the quality or availability of technological services if they are financially
contributing to them.

District 89: Part of Auburn

So, again, I'd appreciate and encourage you to ask questions of the Department. I'd also encourage you to work the bill to ensure that it serves to protect these technological services and the educational programs they sen/e. Thanks,
Adam R. Lee
District 89: Part of Auburn

In Support of:
LD 42, An Act Regarding the Bind-over and Detention of Juveniles

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Criminal Justice and Public Safety, I am Christine Thibeault, Associate Commissioner of the Maine Department of Corrections (DOC) Division of Juvenile Services providing testimony in support of LD 42, An Act Regarding the Bind-
over and Detention of Juveniles. As further explained below, this is a department bill that allows a Juvenile Court judge to authorize detention at Long Creek Youth Development Center ofjuveniles between 18 and 21 years of age during the pendency of a bind-over appeal. The Department thanks Representative Salisbury for sponsoring this bill on our behalf.
The purpose of LD 42 is to expand discretion of Maine's Juvenile Court judges by granting authority to order
detention of j uveniles between 18 and 21 years of age at Long Creek Youth Development Center while the juvenile's appeal of a bind-over order is pending. Fortunately, the number of j uveniles bound-over for prosecution as adults in Maine is small. The impact, however, of having a juvenile detained at a County Jail is significant especially if the Juvenile Court's decision to order bind-over is reversed on appeal. In 2021, the
Juvenile Code, 15 MRSA �3402, sub-�1, 11H, was amended to allow a juvenile to immediately appeal the
issuance of a bind-over order. There was no corresponding change in law, however, that would allow the juvenile to remain at Long Creek pending the outcome of such an appeal.
The Maine Juvenile Code, 15 MRSA �3 101, sub-�4, 11E-2, currently mandates that a person who has reached 18
years of age and has been bound-over for prosecution as an adult be held in an adult section of a jail. The Juvenile Court does not have authority to allow the bound-over juvenile to remain at Long Creek Youth Development Center pending an appeal of the court's decision regardless of the youth's behavior while detained at Long Creek or the potential impact on the youth.
As proposed, LD 42 will allow the Department of Corrections to request that the juvenile remain at Long Creek
pending the outcome of their appeal. Whether the Department makes such a request will depend on the youth's
behavior, engagement with programming, and behavioral health needs. For example, the Department may make such a request because a youth is close to earning a high school diploma, has been attending college classes through the "Creek to College" partnership with Southern Maine Community College, or has behavioral
and/or mental health needs that are more appropriately managed at a juvenile detention facility. Additionally, the Department will consider the impact on other residents of having the bound-over youth remaining at Long
Creek.

This bill simply seeks to expand the discretion of Maine's Juvenile Court judges by eliminating the current mandate that all youths between 18 and 21 years of age be ordered held in an adult-serving jail while an appeal of a bind-over decision is pending. This bill does not mandate that any such youth remain at Long Creek, and it allows the judge to later rescind an order that the youth be detained at Long Creek should the youth's behavior and/or needs change. In short, this bill allows judges to make an individualized decision on where a youth will be housed when an appeal of a bind-over decision is pending.
This concludes my testimony.
I am happy to answer questions.

10031495:
CLAC MEMORANDUM/TESTIMONY NFNA LD 42, An Act Regarding the Bind-over and Detention of Juveniles
TO: Senator Anne Beebe-Center Representative Tavis Hasenfus Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
FR: Criminal Law Advisory Commission (CLAC) c/o laura.yustak@maine.gov
RE: LD 42, An Act Regarding the Bind-over and Detention of Juveniles
DA: January 27, 2025
The Criminal Law Advisory Commission (CLAC)* respectfully submits the following testimony neither for nor against LD 42 as currently drafted.
CLAC supports the aim of the bill, which is to give the Juvenile Court discretion with respect to a juvenile's placement during a potentially narrow time period after a bind-over order, before the juvenile turns 18 or is indicted, and pending any appeal of a bind-over order. CLAC's testimony is neither for nor against, because members identified a number of implementation questions that the Legislature may wish to address.
Members noted that there was no indication of the standard of proof or type of factors to be taken into consideration by the court, and that some of these factors may overlap with those already considered in the bind-over decision itself. See 15 M.R.S. � 3101(4)(D)[factors], (E)[standard of proof]. Accordingly, it may be helpful for the two issues (bind-over and placement pending appeal of bind-over) to be considered as part of the same proceeding, and by the same judge.
The bill appears to contemplate that the issue would be placed before the court by means of a motion or request by the Dept. of Corrections; the timing of such a request is not articulated, as well as the requirement of notice and opportunity to be heard by both the State's and the juvenile's attorneys.
It is logical that a juvenile would remain in a juvenile facility pending the court's consideration of the request, to avoid moving the person between facilities; if this is the intent, it may be helpful to specify this explicitly.
It is not apparent in the bill whether there is an appeal from a decision denying a request to retain a person in a juvenile facility; the Legislature may wish to specify whether or not there is such an appeal. However, the language does provide that the Dept. may subsequently request the court to rescind such an order after it has been granted. Presumably such a request might be made by the Dept. if the juvenile's circumstances or needs change significantly and can longer be met in the juvenile facility, but the standard and factors are not articulated. The Legislature may wish to consider when it is appropriate to bring forward a request to rescind the prior order.

*CLAC is an advisory body established by the Legislature. 17-A M.R.S. �� 1351-1357. It consists of 9 members appointed by the Attorney General. Our current members include defense attorneys, prosecutors, Maine Bar Counsel, and a retired practitioner with experience as defense counsel, prosecutor and in court administration. In addition, three sitting judges and one retired practitioner, appointed by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Judicial Court, and, by statute, the CoChairs of the Legislature's Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety, serve as consultants. The Supreme Judicial Court's Criminal Process Manager serves as liaison from the Court to CLAC. CLAC advises the Legislature on matters relating to crimes in the Criminal Code and in other Titles, the Bail and Juvenile Codes, and with respect to other statutes related to criminal justice processes.

I am writing to express my support for LD 42, a bill that takes important steps toward improving Maine's juvenile justice system. This legislation recognizes that young people are still developing and deserve opportunities for rehabilitation rather than unnecessary detention, especially for non-violent offenses. By limiting the use of detention, strengthening legal protections, and promoting faster court processes, LD 42 helps ensure that youth are treated fairly and are not held longer than necessary. It also encourages the use of community-based programs, education, and counseling, which are proven to reduce repeat offenses and support positive outcomes. Passing LD 42 would move Maine toward a more just, effective, and forward-thinking system that benefits both young people and the broader community.

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the
Committee:
My name is Peter Lehman and I live in Thomaston. I am a formerly incarcerated
citizen and a person in long-term recove1y.* I am testifying neither for nor against
LD 42 on behalf of the Maine Prisoner Advocacy Coalition whose goal is to
promote restorative practices in order to increase public safety and the health of our community.
This bill allows youth ages l8 to 21 who the Juvenile Court has bound over to be
tried as an adult whose trial has not begun to be housed in a DOC juvenile facility
until their trial actually begins or they are sentenced.
MPAC's position is that while this may be more humane than being held in an adult
facility it is nonetheless inhumane and unacceptable for juveniles to be tried as
adults.
The premise of juvenile justice is that youth cannot be held responsible because they are not yet capable of making binding decisions or understanding the long-term
consequences of their actions. This premise is reflected in age of consent laws, voting laws, limits on purchasing or consuming substances, driving and other
licensing laws, not being able to enter into binding contracts, and many others.
Trying juveniles as adults is to treat them as if they were beasts or animals needing
to be "put down" rather than human beings.
Moreover, we know that race, ethnicity, religion, socio-economic status and many
other characteristics are applied in these decisions to try youth as adults. This
compounds the violation of fundamental human rights.
We ask you to remedy this deplorable situation.
Thank you for your attention. I 'm happy to try to answer any questions.

Testimony not for or against LD 42 to the Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety
January 27, 2025
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Committee:
My name is Sarah Johnson and I am a resident of Sanford. I am writing regarding LD 42, An Act Regarding the Bind-over and Detention of Juveniles. I am neither for nor against this bill.
My issue with this bill is that it stands on the premise that juveniles should be tried as adults. Regardless of where they are `housed' until trial, this is simply inhumane, and contrary to any philosophy of juvenile justice. We as a state and a nation have had laws in place for decades prohibiting behaviors by age such as age of consent, voting rights and alcohol consumption, primarily based on our knowledge of brain development and maturity. We now have new research from numerous scientific studies that state adolescent brain development continues into the mid twenties. The Sentencing Project 2023 study "Why Youth Incarceration Fails: An Updated Review of the Evidence" (https://www.sentencingproject.org/reports/why-youth-incarceration-fails-an-updated-review-of-the-evidence/" summarizes the new data: "We now know that the human brain does not fully mature until age 25. Recent advances in brain science have confirmed that the sections of the brain dedicated to impulse control, weighing consequences, and regulating emotions are still developing during adolescence, while the part of the brain focused on sensation-seeking and risk taking is unusually active." The detailed report describes why youth incarceration does not increase public safety, and "Incarceration harms young people's physical and mental health, impedes their educational and career success, and often exposes them to abuse. And the use of confinement is plagued by severe racial and ethnic disparities."
We have solid and growing Restorative Justice organizations in Maine, along with numerous other advocacy groups who support diversion programs for youth. Continuing archaic and inhumane practices of incarcerating youth in Maine is not helping anyone.
I hope you will consider other legislation to promote youth diversion programs. Thank you for your time and consideration. Sarah Johnson Sanford, Maine.

Good aftemoon Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of
the Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety. My name is Sue Salisbury,
and I represent House District 128, which includes part of Westbrook. I am pleased to sponsor
LD 42, An Act Regarding the Bind-over and Detention of Juveniles.
Under current law, a juvenile who is over the age of 18 when a bind-over order is issued must be
transferred to an adult facility. This bill would allow the juvenile to remain in the juvenile
facility pending their appeal to the Law Court of the bind-over decision at the discretion of the

10031308:
Valerie Caruso Augusta LD 42
The concepts of bind-over and detention of juveniles in the context of the justice system both raise important issues regarding the balance between protecting society, ensuring accountability, and recognizing the developmental needs of young people.
Bind-Over "Bind-over" refers to the process in which a juvenile case is transferred from juvenile court to adult court, typically when the offense is particularly severe or when the juvenile is considered to be beyond the rehabilitation goals of the juvenile justice system. In the context of a bind-over, there is often debate about whether it is appropriate to treat juveniles as adults in the criminal justice system.
Pros: Public safety: Bind-over can help ensure that juveniles who commit serious crimes are held accountable in a way that corresponds to the severity of their actions. Deterrence: The prospect of being tried as an adult may act as a deterrent for juveniles considering committing serious crimes. Cons: Developmental immaturity: Juveniles' brains are still developing, especially in areas related to impulse control, decision-making, and understanding long-term consequences. Treating juveniles as adults may fail to account for these developmental differences. Risk of harsher outcomes: Juveniles face harsher sentences in adult court, including longer prison terms and exposure to adult offenders, which can increase the likelihood of re-offending and damage their ability to reintegrate into society. Lack of rehabilitation focus: Juvenile justice systems are typically more focused on rehabilitation and reintegration, whereas adult systems often prioritize punishment over reform. Detention of Juveniles The detention of juveniles involves holding young people in secure facilities pending trial or sentencing. Juvenile detention centers are meant to offer both secure custody and rehabilitative programs, but the practice has faced scrutiny.
Pros:
Safety for the community: Detention can protect the community from juveniles who are deemed to be a danger, particularly if they are involved in violent crimes. Immediate structure: Detention may offer a structured environment where troubled youth can receive educational services, counseling, and support. Cons:
Negative effects on development: Detention, especially in harsh conditions, can exacerbate mental health issues, increase the likelihood of future criminal behavior, and negatively impact educational and social development. Over-reliance on detention: There is a concern that detention is sometimes used inappropriately for minor offenses or for children from marginalized communities. Alternative programs such as diversion, restorative justice, or community-based interventions may be more effective in rehabilitating youth. Separation from family: Detention removes young people from their families and communities, which can impede their social development and support systems. Conclusion Both bind-over and juvenile detention practices require careful consideration of a juvenile's age, maturity, the nature of their offense, and their potential for rehabilitation. It's crucial to balance the need for public safety and accountability with an understanding of the unique developmental characteristics of youth. Ideally, the juvenile justice system should prioritize rehabilitation and consider non-incarceration alternatives, reserving detention and bind-over for cases where they are truly necessary for public safety or justice.
